title: The Real Life Mermaids of Florida’s Weeki Wachee Springs
author: Carolyn Wells
content:
There’s been plenty of coverage on the Weeki Wachee mermaids in recent years, and Jack Burke isn’t trying to break any new ground here. But he does manage to bring to life the weird underground theatre where the mermaids have danced for decades, beautifully evoking the wonder of celestial blue light and sparkly tails. Burke’s piece is a gentle homage to “this weird little relic from another age”—a time in America that belonged to the hustlers and the dreamers.

I eventually find a seat in the auditorium, just as a video of Mr Margaritaville himself, Jimmy Buffett, crackles onto the wall-mounted televisions. He launches into a rendition of Fins, featuring a quartet of smiling and costumed Weeki Wachee mermaids being wheeled on stage to backing-dance from their seats. Around me are grandparents in visors, sunburnt dads in fishing shirts, and little girls in glittering mermaid tails clutching plush dolphins.

The lights dim and a syrupy-voiced MC asks us if we’re ready for the mermaids. Inevitably, we are not quite ready enough, and are encouraged to express our excitement a little more vocally.

The dusty blue satin curtain slowly winches itself open, to reveal a thick wall of glass, behind which lies the famous spring itself. A water so clear and turquoise it hardly looks like water at all. Schools of tiny fish drift lazily across the scene. A turtle paddles past with supreme indifference.

And then, rising out of some deeper part of the spring, comes a mermaid.

title: Isolated, Scared, Forlorn: The Heartbreaking Final Months of Virginia Giuffre’s Life
author: Seyward Darby
content:
Virginia Giuffre made global headlines for her fight against her sexual abusers among the wealthy elite, all detailed in a bestselling memoir. Now new questions have emerged about the private anguish the most famous accuser of Jeffrey Epstein faced at home. Her husband, whom she once credited with helping her escape Epstein, had assaulted and tormented her for years:

On March 4, 2015, police attended the Giuffre home after receiving several 911 hang-up calls. According to the police report, Virginia said she tried to stop Robbie punching and kicking their dog, Bear, which Robbie said had bitten him. She said Robbie then punched her several times in her face and head, grabbed her by the throat, and strangled her. Virginia had a bruise forming on her left cheek, blood on her sleeve, and a whitish-clear fluid mixed with blood leaking from her ear, which police noted could be cerebral spinal fluid, a symptom of severe head trauma. Robbie was arrested on domestic violence charges and taken to jail, where he told an officer he’d hit Virginia by accident.

Dale King, the then-detective sergeant who went to check on Virginia the next morning… [says] he remembers Robbie flagged him down in the street. He knew the couple because he’d been to the house to keep the paparazzi in line and investigate the strange break-ins. King said Robbie seemed to be soothing himself with a story he’d heard him narrate before, about being the savior. “He’s trying to convince me that I have to let him get back home so he can protect her,” he says. “Hell,” he remembers thinking. “You’re her biggest threat right now.”

title: A Strange Continent
author: Carolyn Wells
content:
Ben Markovits, an Austin-raised writer long settled in London, returns home with his teenage son and a pair of folding bikes for a ride through the Hill Country. As they pedal from Pedernales Falls toward Salt Lick BBQ, the shifting Texas landscape prompts reflections on English density versus Texan sprawl and on the deeper divide between the two cultures. By journey’s end, Markovits is left reckoning with how places—and our idea of “home”—keep changing, even as we try to return to them, a question that lingers long after the ride is over.

I had hoped, while my kids were still kids, that we’d live in Texas for a year, that they’d know something of my childhood—not just America generally, but something about the neighborhood I grew up in and the space and the year-round warm weather that makes childhood an outdoor sport, and not an indoor one as it is in England from October onward. But it didn’t happen. My daughter is now at university, and my son, 16, is caught up in the two-year cycles of English high school exams. This means the window where this move is still possible for us has closed—except for the one week over Christmas when we fly to Austin and my kids can pretend, in the company of their American cousins, to be Texans.

title: Beckett the Prophet
author: Brendan Fitzgerald
content:
The peg for Robert Zaretsky’s essay on Samuel Beckett’s Waiting for Godot feels flimsy: “the 70th anniversary of its American premiere,” which lagged the show’s proper premiere, in Paris, by three years. Disregard the peg; as Zaretsky makes clear, there’s not a bad time, these days, to consider Beckett’s best-known work, a demonstration of “solidarity and compassion” set against a “featureless, colorless vista.” The stage directions for Godot have Estragon, one of the play’s leads, look out into the auditorium as an extension of the devastation. “Inspiring prospects,” he says. Let’s hope so.

Of course, Godot never arrives. In a Sesame Street parody of the play, the tree, fed up with the melodramatic and nonsensical patter of two Muppets waiting for Elmo, uproots itself and walks off the stage. But we cannot uproot ourselves and walk off the stage; instead, stuck like Didi and Gogo in a state of non-arrival, we wait. For those who waited for an answer from Beckett, none ever came. He once snapped at the English actor Ralph Richardson, who asked if Godot stood for God. If he had meant God, Beckett said, he would have written God. The play, he insisted, strove to avoid definition. This strategy of avoidance leaves us to gaze at a landscape void of meaning, one that by turns is the source of our bemusement and amusement.

title: Slay the Spire 2 developers detail art and animation work behind Aeonglass, the game's fourth Act 3 boss that replaced Doormaker
author: Fran Ruiz
content:
Rotating ideas.

Last month, Slay the Spire 2's Act 3 boss Doormaker - the third in a series of late-game reworks - was removed and replaced by Aeonglass. Now, developer Mega Crit has revealed how its fun visual design came to be.

Slay the Spire 2 is now in the middle of its early access journey, and developer Mega Crit has a pretty solid cadence of updates, many of which have reworked and even removed bosses in an attempt to perfect the roguelike deckbuilder's gameplay loop and level of challenge. Act 3 is one part of the game that's already had four different bosses, and while we don't know for sure if Aeonglass will make it to 1.0, its hourglass-inspired design is among the game's most visually arresting yet.

In a recent Steam blog post, Mega Crit animator Chris Gortz explained the team explored different concepts following Doormaker, "including a multi-faceted pillar of death that could rotate its sections to reveal different capabilities". Such concepts were apparently envisioned as an upgrade of Doormaker's 'rocky portal' design, but the team eventually moved away from that.

The post reveals five different Aeonglass designs - all different takes on the concept of a killer hourglass - with option B emerging victorious after some debate. "I did some tests to make sure I could simulate 3D rotating metal rings in 2D space. The result wasn't much to look at, but as a proof of concept it worked well enough for us to move ahead," Gortz explained. To figure out its combat style, doodles helped, and the concept of "a big atom" with blast and slice attacks took form.

Art director Marlowe Dobbe also "requested that the stuff in the hourglass move more like lava lamp goo than the traditional sand", which pushed Gortz to use the same smoke shader as for the body of the Living Smog boss. The end result is very effective.

The most recent beta patch has already nerfed Aeonglass' front-loaded damage and swapped some of its animations, so expect more changes to hit the Act 3 boss in the future even if they stick around.

Slay the Spire 2 isn't expected to exit Steam early access until 2027 at the earliest, as the first game took one-and-a-half-years to fully flesh out. Console releases haven't been confirmed but should be expected around the time of its eventual 1.0 update.

Eurogamer's early access review of Slay the Spire 2 noted that "Mega Crit demonstrates that it absolutely understands what makes this eccentric card game crackle and fizz, and why so many people enjoy playing it."

title: Charli XCX and the Strokes Are (Sort of) Making Rock Music
author: @NewYorker
content:
Last week, Charli XCX and the Strokes, twin pillars of a certain strain of disaffected, irony-drenched cool, each released new records that flirt with the idea of “rock music.” In both cases, the deliberate garbling of genre feels like a pointed disavowal: rock music, in particular, has long been preoccupied with notions of authenticity and defiance. In the case of Charli XCX, the smart and funny hyperpop singer whose sixth album, “BRAT,” became a multidimensional cultural phenomenon in 2024, she seems to be attempting to shake off an overdetermined, übercommodified version of herself. On “Rock Music,” the first single from “Music, Fashion, Film,” her new album, and the follow-up to “BRAT” (not counting a soundtrack she released this year, to the Emerald Fennell-directed adaptation of “Wuthering Heights”), Charli sings:

I think the dance floor is deadSo now we’re making rock musicWow, I’m really banging my headI’m really hurting my neck

Of course, “Rock Music” is not “rock music” in the traditional sense, though Charli’s vocals are clipped, punkish, and dry, buoyed by a crunch of guitar. (Her sarcastic delivery of the word “wow” contains all the casual but devastating disdain of an angsty preteen.) Stylistically, the song is a twitchy mix of E.D.M. and grunge—more akin to LCD Soundsystem than, say, Pearl Jam. In an Instagram post from May, containing some behind-the-scenes footage of its creation, she wrote, “a video of me making a song called ‘rock music’ that is not actually rock music which is funny because i never said i was making a rock album.” O.K.! One complication of being ultra-chic and eye-roll-y is that, after a while, it becomes impossible for your public to tell which end is up. Or, as John Updike once wrote, “Celebrity is a mask that eats into the face.”

Mostly, “Music, Fashion, Film” is ad hoc and confessional, undercooked in a way that feels both pleasing and purposeful. It contains just eleven songs and clocks in at around thirty minutes. Lyrically, the album is preoccupied with legacy, perception, and mortality. (The cover features a staid black-and-white portrait of John Cale, Marc Jacobs, and Martin Scorsese—living titans of music, fashion, and film, respectively.) Its guitars are scuzzy and immediate, and the production, by Charli, A. G. Cook, and Finn Keane, her longtime collaborators, is unpredictable and sometimes surprisingly visceral. “Magic Metal Montana,” one of the album’s best tracks, is a tenderhearted paean to her friendship with Cook: “I’d be nothing without you / I think you taught me, I think I taught you / You believe me, I believe you,” she sings. The softness in her voice is disarming, even through layers of effects.

Charli’s work has always toggled between true vulnerability and hedonistic self-aggrandizement. On the chorus of “360,” a single from “BRAT,” Charli boasts about her ubiquity: “When you’re in the mirror you’re just looking at me / I’m everywhere, I’m so Julia,” she sings, an IYKYK reference to the downtown icon Julia Fox. Yet on “Sympathy is a Knife,” a song purportedly about Taylor Swift, she admitted to feeling goosey, small: “ ’Cause I couldn’t even be her if I tried / I’m opposite, I’m on the other side.” Swift, who can be terrifyingly vicious with her detractors, seemed to respond a year later with “Actually Romantic,” a weird and petty song co-written with Max Martin and Shellback: “I heard you call me Boring Barbie when the coke’s got you brave,” Swift chirped. Their alleged feud was equal parts funny and mortifying, as it often is when privileged grownups take swings at each other.

In recent years, Charli has adopted a postmodern, almost scholarly interest in fame. It’s hard to say whether she thinks celebrity is more interesting than the work that enables it; at times, her discography has seemed to imply meaning rather than provide it. In a Substack post from this past fall, she linked to a 1974 video of Lou Reed giving an ornery press conference in Sydney, ahead of an Australian tour. Reed wears sunglasses, a lemon-yellow T-shirt, and a popped collar; his hair is short and bleached. He seems to regard the scrum of reporters with a mix of apathy and bafflement. Occasionally, he takes a sip from a glass of juice, using two straws at once. “I don’t have anything to say,” he shrugs, when a journalist pushes him on his terseness. The clip is sometimes recalled as combative, though Reed has the calm but bewildered comportment of someone who has parachuted into a foreign land, and is peering around for the first time. It’s possible that he was on drugs, although, as Charli writes, “Who fucking cares? In my opinion it’s just funny and cool.”

It is funny and cool, though perhaps not just that. The famously idiosyncratic and testy Reed was surely right to eschew spokesperson status. Charli, too, seems to constantly be at odds with her persona. On “No One Lasts Forever,” another new song, she sings:

Everyone thinks I’ve got a problemSince everyone knows my nameThat I’m irresponsible and rudeThat I’ll put thе drugs in my veins

The end of the song has an appearance from the filmmaker and body-horror auteur David Cronenberg, who recounts a near-death experience he had after collapsing on the street, near his home in Toronto. “As I was lying there on the sidewalk, I did not think about art at all,” Cronenberg says. “I thought about people—I thought about life.” I couldn’t quite tell if Charli included the outro as a rejoinder to her own philosophy, which seems to center art—or, at least, being perceived as an Artist—above all else. Or if perhaps she was trying to tell us that she, too, sees creativity as separate, heightened, and divorced from humanity, yet wholly meaningless without it.

When the Strokes put out their début LP, “Is This It,” in 2001, they were instantly, breathlessly anointed as saviors of New York City’s sagging rock scene. Even back then, they seemed hugely uninterested in that title. (The summer before the record’s release, a journalist from the NME suggested to the front man, Julian Casablancas, that his band might single-handedly revive the genre: “That’s fucking ridiculous,” Casablancas, then twenty-two, replied.) I still love “Is This It,” a punchy album about being young and bratty and terrified and also totally sure of yourself. Since 2001, though, the Strokes have often appeared on the verge of psychic dissolution—shortly before their June tour, the guitarist Nick Valensi announced that he was taking a “temporary break” from the band—and they have yet to make another record quite as pure and potent as that first one.

Yet, in some ways, Casablancas has only become more interesting, both as a vocalist and as an irascible, often controversial front man. “Reality Awaits,” the Strokes’ seventh and strangest album, came out the same day as “Music, Fashion, Film.” It was preceded by two singles, “Going Shopping” and “Falling Out of Love,” both of which caused a mild hubbub for the aggressive use of Auto-Tune on Casablancas’s doe-eyed warble. (“Reality Awaits” was produced by Rick Rubin, who is known simultaneously for his subtractive, Zen-like minimalism and for making things sound compressed and preposterously loud; he does both here.) I surprised myself by eating up the Auto-Tune; much like on Bon Iver’s “715 - CRΣΣKS,” which has Justin Vernon singing through a bespoke pitch-shifting vocal processor known as the Messina, the prismatic splintering of Casablancas’s voice has a kind of surreal, iridescent quality. “More human than human,” as Rob Zombie once sang. Lyrically, Casablancas, like Charli XCX, seesaws between raw sincerity and who-gives-a-fuck insouciance, and his mutant vocals bridge those two modes of being. I laughed out loud at a verse on “Lonely in the Future,” in which a loose and unbothered Casablancas fires off a series of seemingly random potshots, including a dig at Harry Styles, whose “As It Was” uses a beat similar to that of the Strokes’ “Hard to Explain”:

Weeknd, I like your outfitYOLO, you only live onceDude kept the beat “As It Was”John Legend, that’s Josh GrobanI guess I’m flattered, maybeAll good, we all steal, baby

Why not riff on celebrity and the distorting nature of fame in a lightly robotic voice? Casablancas, too, is channelling Lou Reed in Sydney, refusing to soften his crankiness or his illegibility: “I did that yesterday, when I was a kid,” he sings on “Lonely in the Future.” Yet, elsewhere on the record, he sounds beautifully unguarded. “Falling Out of Love” seems to be about what happens after a relationship ends—all the feelings that linger before transforming into something new. “I’m in love with a ghost / I’ll be always and never alone,” he sings. Again like Charli, he is trying to decide what parts of his life are real and spiritually sustainable. On the song’s half-spoken second verse, the Auto-Tune subsides a little, and Casablancas’s tone resembles that of Matt Berninger, of the National—deep, gritty, resigned.

There’s something fundamentally warped about both “Music, Fashion, Film” and “Reality Awaits”—some emptiness or corruption lurking at their centers, threatening to take hold—but it hasn’t prevented me from enjoying the albums. This perhaps speaks to my own degradation, or to the generally rotten state of the world right now. “The worse reality gets, the less you want to hear about it,” Casablancas sings on “Going Shopping.” It’s a finger-wag of a lyric, but of course he’s also right. Each of these records wonders how art can, or should, respond to danger. In the past, rock has done that by being dangerous itself. Here, it seems, the sound of that threat has changed: it’s more about inhabiting and manipulating the machine than about raging against it. ♦

title: Marco Rubio Takes Aim at Globalists and the Left
author: @NewYorker
content:
In August, 2022, Viktor Orbán, Hungary’s then Prime Minister, travelled to Dallas in a bid to save “Western civilization.” The opening speech he delivered at that year’s Conservative Political Action Conference called for the defeat of “the globalist ruling class,” and urged greater coördination between nationalist forces on both sides of the Atlantic. Orbán offered his American audience a bit of advice from his many years in office, during which he had bullied civil society, stacked the judiciary, bent state media to his whims, and waged a relentless culture war against the left. “In order to win, it is not enough to know what you’re fighting for,” Orbán told the CPAC crowd. “You should also know how you should fight. My answer is: play by your own rules.”

Orbán’s winning run ended this April, in a landslide defeat in national elections, but his template for victory endures. The second term of President Donald Trump can be read as an exercise in speed-running through Orbán’s playbook, with the Administration attacking universities, chipping away at the independence of mainstream media outlets, and attempting to better gerrymander districts in favor of the Republican Party, among other things. Trump’s top lieutenants also evidently see themselves engaged in a profoundly ideological contest. In recent days, Secretary of State Marco Rubio has presided over a number of initiatives to combat perceived “anti-American” threats. Last week, he announced renewed efforts to unravel the International Criminal Court, which the State Department described in a press release as a “globalist” menace that represents “an intolerable threat to U.S. sovereignty.” He also convened a conference in Washington, attended by representatives from more than sixty nations, though few top diplomats, on the supposed danger of global “far-left” terrorism, and encouraged other governments to join the United States to help “crush this evil forever.” And, on Monday, the State Department issued a hundred-page report on Cuba that links communist-influence operations to protest movements, activists, and politicians in the country, including members of the Democratic Socialists of America and New York City’s mayor, Zohran Mamdani.

The timing for all this is curious. The Trump Administration—faced with plummeting approval ratings, a potential major electoral setback in the November midterms, and a war in the Middle East that it should never have started, doesn’t know how to end, and seems in the process of renewing—may be searching for new distractions to invigorate its base and occupy the news cycle. But Rubio’s gambits still reflect an agenda that has always animated this White House; the President started picking fights with the I.C.C. during his first term, while Rubio, a Cuban American with a large constituency from the same background in South Florida, has long dreamed of regime change in Havana. Taken together in the current moment, though, the moves point to a kind of intensification of MAGA’s illiberal project, a process that Rubio appears eager to lead.

Rubio put the I.C.C. on notice with a video message and an opinion piece published in the Wall Street Journal, and vowed to “systemically disable” it. The spur of Rubio’s ire may be the court’s ongoing war-crimes case against the Israeli Prime Minister, Benjamin Netanyahu; neither Israel nor the United States is a party to the Rome Statute that brought the court into being, in 2002, but Israel’s devastation of Gaza gives the court jurisdiction on the issue, since Palestine is a formal member. There’s an active I.C.C. warrant for Netanyahu’s arrest, which Mamdani, in a video posted on Tuesday evening, said that he wished to execute when the Israeli leader next comes to New York City, likely in September, but that he has no “legal authority” to do so independent of federal authorities. The Trump Administration attacked Mamdani for his stance. There are also campaigns from human-rights groups to get the court to consider war crimes against the United States for its strikes on alleged narco-traffickers in the Caribbean and on civilian targets in Iran, though no formal investigations, let alone charges, seem imminent. There was an investigation, launched in 2020, into alleged U.S. war crimes in Afghanistan, but the I.C.C. recently moved to “deprioritise” it. Generations of U.S. lawmakers have balked at allowing the I.C.C. jurisdiction over this country, but no official has embarked on such a sweeping attack on the institution as Rubio, who wants to expand existing anti-I.C.C. sanctions—which already include travel bans, asset freezes, and other restrictions on a number of I.C.C. personnel working on cases involving U.S. and Israeli nationals—and to pressure other nations to withdraw from the court altogether. Kenneth Roth, an American attorney and the former executive director of Human Rights Watch, told me that at stake could be the very principle of whether “governments control prosecution of crimes on their territory,” which he described as a basic element of justice. “The Trump Administration would have people believe that, if I commit a war crime in London, it somehow violates national sovereignty for Britain to allow the I.C.C. to prosecute me,” he said.

The targeting of the I.C.C. is part of the Trump Administration’s broader friction with major parts of the international system, which U.S. officials frequently argue is somehow rigged against American interests and beholden to “woke” agendas. It has pulled out of some United Nations treaties and agencies—including the Paris Climate Accords and the World Health Organization—while it is more broadly championing budget cuts across the U.N. and the streamlining or paring down of affiliated agencies and international organizations, as well as efforts to supplant them with its own initiatives, such as Trump’s quixotic Board of Peace. But the campaign to break the I.C.C., Stewart Patrick, a senior fellow at the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace, wrote, “is a campaign of pure destruction, a coercive attempt to impose the United States’ will on the rest of the world.” Prominent U.S. allies, including the French President, Emmanuel Macron, have spoken in defense of the I.C.C., and it’s unclear how much traction Rubio’s offensive will gain. John B. Bellinger III, a former legal adviser to the State Department during the George W. Bush Administration, sees the initiative “as a political message intended for a domestic audience.”

The same is true for the summit arranged by the State Department last week on the spectral menace of alleged far-left terrorist organizations. There, too, Rubio touted a campaign to “dismantle” his quarry—in this case, far-left activist networks that he sees as coördinating activities from Europe to the Americas. He suggested that “Antifa militants” are a graver threat than Islamist extremists, and summoned a history of left-wing violence primarily from the nineteen-seventies to make his argument. (Trump’s Justice Department, meanwhile, has quietly deleted a 2024 department study, which found far-right extremists were involved in far more ideologically motivated killings than their left-wing or Islamist counterparts.) Last year, the White House released a national-security memorandum about targeting “domestic terrorism,” which the American Civil Liberties Union described as “a fever dream of conspiracies” and “outright falsehoods” set up to target or suppress the work of myriad left-leaning activists, nonprofits, and their donors. Separately, the Trump Administration placed four European “Antifa” factions—two from Greece, one from Italy, and one from Germany—on its State Department foreign-terrorist-organizations list, a set of designations that left many European officials bemused, not least because of the lingering vagueness behind who or what even constitutes “Antifa.” At the conference, Rubio said that the left is “a distinctive and unique evil. It has always been driven by a hatred above all else, a hatred for civilization itself. It is a revolt of the worst against the best, a revolt of the weak and the cowardly against the strong and the good. It is perpetrated by those who cannot build, who cannot create, who cannot achieve great things, and take their revenge upon the world for their own inadequacy by seeking to destroy those who can.”

Critics of an Administration that pardoned the January 6th insurrectionists see this as shameless, cynical grandstanding. “We strongly urge the Department to return its focus to a serious mission set that is definitionally apolitical, data-driven, and rooted in reality,” a letter, which eleven Democratic lawmakers wrote to Rubio, said. You could read the Secretary of State’s ideological fervor as smoke from the fire of an Administration that’s eroding traditional checks and balances and using whatever coercive instruments it has to get its way, Roth said. “This is a lawless Administration, and that effort to put itself above the law manifests itself in various ways,” he said. Damian Murphy, the senior vice-president for national security and international policy at the Center for American Progress, a center-left think tank, warned that such rhetoric coming from the top echelons of U.S. leadership only “serves to embolden those illiberal actors who oftentimes use the guise of counterterrorism as a way to exert authoritarian control, which we’ve seen over and over in places like Russia, in places like China.” He also added that “our counterterrorism resources are finite. So when time and resources are spent targeting weak groups that pose little, if any, threat to the United States, it really calls into question the political motivations behind this effort.”

Rubio isn’t hiding his motivations in the Caribbean. In a post on X, he said that the State Department’s new Cuba report, which is titled “Cuba: The Capital of 21st Century Communism,” presents a full accounting of Havana’s ties to American “radical leftism and Third Worldism” which “the American people deserve to know.” The report offers a potted history of the Communist regime’s influence campaigns, threading a needle between its early support of groups such as the Black Panthers to current “ties to powerful leftist nonprofits, anti-ICE collectives, socialist groups, and Marxist militant organizations across the United States.” The report can be read as another broadside against the American left, but it’s also part of the Trump Administration’s escalating approach to Cuba, which is under a punishing oil blockade and could yet face a U.S. military incursion. Michael Bustamante, a historian of Cuba at the University of Miami, told me that the report offers “a compendium of the greatest hits of allegations of Cuban subversion over time,” which, while not entirely inaccurate, is selective in its composition. He also noted the American right’s long tradition of attempting to scapegoat legitimate protest with accusations of foreign influence. “It’s not for nothing that organizations like the John Birch Society in the sixties used to see civil rights writ large as this kind of communist conspiracy with links to Havana and Moscow, and so it’s really sad to see that recirculated in this way, in this overly simplistic fashion,” he said.

The Administration’s opponents are troubled. In recent days, “Rubio has launched two equally ambitious campaigns—the first is a rejuvenated McCarthy Red Scare campaign at home to hunt down left-wing activists who oppose this Administration’s agenda, and the other is to align its allies at global scale toward this anti-left agenda,” David Adler, an American activist who is a co-coördinator of the Progressive International, a global network of left-wing political parties, unions, and movements, told me. He pointed to the Panamerican Congress, a summit of left-wing politicians and diplomats that will be held in Uruguay next month, as an example of burgeoning efforts to push back against Trump and Rubio’s apparent desire for hemispheric hegemony. (Representative Pramila Jayapal, a Democrat from Washington State, is expected to lead a U.S. delegation there.)

Whether Rubio’s campaigns prove effective is a separate matter. Opinion polls show the U.S.’s favorability under Trump at record lows around the world, including among its traditional allies. The White House’s blustering over Greenland and meddling in the Persian Gulf have also compelled European far-right factions otherwise in its camp to distance themselves from Trump’s policy goals and agenda. On the Continent, the Trump brand is toxic, even if Rubio’s rhetoric may find some sympathetic ears. In Budapest, Orbán, before his electoral defeat, announced his intention to pull Hungary out of the I.C.C., a gesture made with Netanyahu standing beside him and, it seems, likely coördinated with the Trump Administration. In May, Hungary’s new parliament voted to reverse that decision. Péter Magyar, Orbán’s rival and successor, has said that if Netanyahu returns to Hungary, his government would be obliged to take the Israeli leader into custody. ♦

title: Gassed Up
author: Krista Stevens
content:
Before I read this piece, all I knew about tomatoes was that homegrown tastes infinitely better than store-bought. For Offrange, Mitch Hagney educated me on how tomatoes ripen naturally and unnaturally, and how Big Tomato forces the issue in huge warehouses by pumping in ethylene gas. It might just inspire you to grow your own.

Tomatoes are climacteric fruits, like bananas, avocados, and mangos, which means they can be harvested unripe and complete the process later. Ethylene sends the hormonal signal to ripen. When that process happens naturally, cells near its seeds start producing the gas and it diffuses outward through the fruit. Each cell the gas reaches begins its own production, and the cascade softens the flesh and the tomato turns red from the inside out. That allows the fruit to be picked much greener, shipped far, and then ripened when they’re close to their eater.

To do it artificially isn’t complicated, but it is expensive. Ethylene floods the room at carefully calibrated amounts, and the operator compresses what might take weeks into five days. Sensors log temperature, humidity, and gas concentrations around the clock. The tomato turns red from the outside in.

More picks about farming

Black Earth

Christina Cooke | The Bitter Southerner | November 25, 2024 | 8,027 words

“In North Carolina, a Black farmer purchased the plantation where his ancestors were enslaved— and is reclaiming his family’s story, his community’s health, and the soil beneath his feet.”

Know Your Burger

David Cook | Oxford American | April 11, 2025 | 2,429 words

“A true farm-to-table story.”

The Price of Eggs

Christopher Solomon | Orion | April 16, 2025 | 2,959 words

“The chickens had arrived the previous spring, unasked for, like most of life’s obligations.”

title: Should We Do More to Fight Looks-Based Discrimination?
author: @NewYorker
content:
In 2007, Miranda Fricker, a British philosopher, published a book called “Epistemic Injustice: Power and the Ethics of Knowing.” It became a smash hit, philosophically speaking, because it diagnosed a problem that had been hard to put into words. Imagine that you witness a crime, Fricker wrote, but find that the police won’t credit your testimony because of the color of your skin. Or suppose you’re being tormented by someone in power, but lack the ability to explain to others—or even to yourself—exactly how you’re being wronged. (You might be like the women in “Mad Men,” who were being sexually harassed by their bosses but lacked the term “sexual harassment.”) These two kinds of injury seem different but are actually related, Fricker argued, because they both have to do with knowledge. In the first case, you know something, but no one will listen to you; in the second, you have trouble fully knowing what’s going on in your life. In either case, you’re suffering from an unfairness of knowledge that limits what you’re able to communicate, what others are willing to hear from you, or what you can understand about yourself and your circumstances.

In the years since the appearance of Fricker’s book, the effort to overcome bias and discrimination has acquired a new flavor. In this latest phase, many harms that were once difficult to describe have been given names, so that they can be better identified and confronted. (We now talk about mansplaining, microaggressions, and gaslighting.) Populations that might not otherwise have seen what they have in common—neurodivergent people, or patients with contested diagnoses—have formed identities and found cause for solidarity. It can be life-changing to have a name for what harms you; society can shift when new groups assert themselves. And yet the pursuit of epistemic justice also risks what the psychologist Nick Haslam has called concept creep—“the progressive expansion of concepts of harm.” The new terms or categories that some find liberating might not reflect an underlying reality. (Not all patients with contested diagnoses face the same struggle.) A new identity can create burdens that aren’t easily shrugged off.

“I have never, until now, confessed to anyone that I felt I was ugly,” the journalist Stephanie Fairyington writes in her new book, “Ugly: A Letter to My Daughter.” Since childhood, she’s felt unattractive; she’s also found it “hard to say the words I am ugly or even I am seen as ugly.” When she’s succeeded in giving voice to such ideas, perhaps using softened language (“My looks aren’t my strong suit”), well-meaning people are quick to disagree, telling her that she looks good. But she’s certain that this isn’t true, and that her appearance has shaped her life. She recalls a moment from her childhood, on “a sunny day in 1986,” when the mother of a friend, parked in a minivan, leaned out the window and exclaimed, incredulously, “That’s Chrysí’s daughter?” Fairyington’s mother and brother were notably good-looking. “Where they had full lips, I had thin ones,” she writes. “Where they had aquiline noses, I had a bulbous red one.” Moreover, “it wasn’t just my face that made me unattractive . . . it was also the legibility of my queerness.”

Fairyington cites the philosopher Thomas J. Spiegel, who, in a paper from 2022, argued that “lookism”—discrimination based on unattractiveness—is not just unfair in itself but also a form of epistemic injustice. Lookism’s existence is beyond dispute: research has shown that pretty people have an easier time making money, finding partners, and even succeeding in court, while unattractive people are judged more harshly, treated more meanly, and seen as lower performing. Yet there is a “taboo” around the subject of ugliness, Spiegel writes, that leads us to hide from ourselves the toll it takes on individuals. Lookism “does not generate the same awareness as gender or race-based discrimination partially for the reason that there is a different kind of discomfort associated with being identified as ugly,” he writes.

“Ugly” is an ugly word. It’s painful to point it at yourself, and cruel to point it at others. It’s also a complicated word, since, as Fairyington shows in her wide-ranging book, beauty and ugliness are not just aesthetic ideas—they have cultural, biological, subjective, intersubjective, political, commercial, and historical dimensions. All this contributes to the fact that there’s no National Association for Unattractive People. No one urges H.R. departments to hold training sessions on overcoming lookism in the workplace; schools don’t teach kids about the costs of lauding beauty and denigrating its opposite. This gap in our defenses against bias may be understandable—but it leaves lookism unnamed and unopposed. What would it take for us to face the problem directly?

The writer Ted Chiang imagines a solution to lookism in the short story “Liking What You See: A Documentary.” In his near-future scenario, it’s become easy and cheap to get your brain modified so that you don’t notice facial beauty. Someone who’s undergone the reversible procedure, which is called calliagnosia—kalos is the Greek word for beauty—“can tell the difference between a pointed chin and a receding one, a straight nose and a crooked one, clear skin and blemished skin,” a neurologist explains. But “he or she simply doesn’t experience any aesthetic reaction to those differences.” The story’s protagonist, a college freshman named Tamera, had the procedure done when she was a child, because her progressive parents were against lookism. Gazing into the mirror, she can’t tell if she’s pretty. It’s only when someone else sees a picture of her with her ex-boyfriend that she learns that she’s out of his league.

At Tamera’s college, an organization called Students for Equality Everywhere, or SEE, wants to amend the school’s code of conduct so that calliagnosia is mandatory. They argue that it makes no sense to fight racism and sexism while tolerating lookism. They also point out that young people are pawns in a technological-arms race. In the story, generative video technology is being used to make models, spokespeople, and politicians unnaturally persuasive, charismatic, and beautiful. An advocate of calliagnosia says that, while it’s reasonable to enjoy looking at ordinary beautiful people, these digital manipulations conjure the equivalent of “pharmaceutical-grade beauty”—“the cocaine of good looks.” Various people in Chiang’s story proffer all sorts of arguments, philosophical, practical, and aesthetic, against blocking the perception of human beauty. But others decide to fight fire with fire, or embrace the technology on philosophical grounds. “The foundations of our culture were laid in classical Greece, where physical beauty and the body were celebrated,” a religion professor at the college explains. “But our culture is also thoroughly permeated by the monotheistic tradition, which devalues the body in favor of the soul.”

It’s interesting to consider how our present-day world compares with Chiang’s fictional one. Like the students in his story, we’re living in an age of technologically accelerated lookism. In our sci-fi reality, those with the means can use GLP-1s to become ultra-slim; they can employ cosmetic surgery to reverse signs of aging, and to redesign their faces and bodies so that they reflect algorithmically adjudicated images of “perfection.” Dating websites reduce people to photographs, even as photo editing gets easier; the video-conferencing apps we use for work offer to enhance our appearances. We are, quite literally, surrounded by “pharmaceutical-grade beauty.” And yet our world, unlike the one in the story, does not offer an equivalent of calliagnosia. Although there are some circumstances in which we can make “blind” decisions—in ninth grade, I auditioned for the school orchestra from behind a curtain—for the most part, our predicament is worse than theirs.

We might, therefore, conclude that we have no choice but to confront lookism head on. What would that effort look like? In her book “The Beauty Bias: The Injustice of Appearance in Life and Law,” from 2010, the legal scholar Deborah L. Rhode proposed that appearance ought to be added to current anti-discrimination laws. Today, there are jurisdictions, across the country, in which discrimination based on height and weight is specifically outlawed; only a handful of statutes use words such as “appearance.” We might imagine a world in which people more regularly sue their employers for appearance-based discrimination. (But would that be a better world?) In the past, it was not unusual to include a photograph of yourself when you submitted a résumé—an obvious vector for lookism—but the hiring process has evolved. Photographs are often prohibited, and anonymized applications and structured interviews have become more commonplace. And yet the consequences of such measures are hard to predict. There is some evidence that they lead to the hiring of candidates who end up performing better at work. But a study conducted by the Australian government, based on “blind” hiring practices in the Australian Public Service, found that they had unpredictable effects on bias, in part because “de-identification may frustrate efforts aimed at promoting diversity.”

In “Beauty Pays: Why Attractive People Are More Successful,” from 2011, the economist Daniel Hamermesh attempts to estimate the “beauty premium”: he suggests that attractive people earn about a hundred and forty thousand dollars more than regular people over a lifetime. (The effect is “not small, it’s not huge,” Hamermesh has said.) In a concluding section, he weighs various options for compensating or protecting those who are denied that premium. One challenge is that attractiveness unfolds along a spectrum, rather than in categories; if the whole bottom third of the spectrum were protected, it would be the largest protected class in society. Even if it existed, would it be a class that people wanted to join?

Moral progress isn’t confined to legislation, of course. It also happens individually and interpersonally; it’s created and promulgated one person at a time, through conversation. In “Ugly,” Fairyington shows how she and her spouse, Sabrina, have tried to give their daughter the tools she’ll need to perceive and resist lookism. In ways both sophisticated and simple—visiting museums, going shopping, listening to Le Tigre—they offer their child a rich understanding of the forces that shape our relationships with our corporeal selves. Their conversations can be hyper-intellectual: “Teasing apart your friend’s ‘fat’ comment, I thought about how the neo-Assyrians preferred heaviness over thinness,” Fairyington writes. But they’re also frank and revelatory; often, they move from questions about bodies or body image into discussions of history, politics, and the broader human experience. As a parent myself, I found the book inspiring.

Around the time he published “Beauty Pays,” Hamermesh did a Q. & A. with readers of the blog “Freakonomics.” “Take advantage of what you’re good at—other things in which you have a comparative advantage,” he told a reader who asked about “how to utterly defeat pretty people.” “Looks are only one of many things that affect success,” he went on. Although Hamermesh was speaking in the language of economics, this isn’t too different from some of what Fairyington puts into practice. An important way to fight lookism is by recognizing human multidimensionality. Like all forms of prejudice, lookism flattens people; we can resist it by being curious, open-minded, and expansive. We can notice that giving in to lookism—a harm we can inflict by degrees, and visit upon ourselves—becomes easier when we use technologies that encourage shallow relationships and assessments.

Does this require us to break the taboo around ugliness—to name it, as Fairyington does? Reading her story, I found myself uncertain. Throughout the book, Fairyington uses the word “ugly” to speak with clarity and force about unfairness. Hearing the term directed at her in middle school was “a new kind of painful,” and it “solidified my ugly self-concept”; at the same time, it “provided a weird kind of relief to know, unequivocally, that my self-understanding was accurate.”

And yet, as Fairyington’s narrative shows, the self-understanding she achieved as a middle schooler wasn’t accurate. Back then, she heard “ugly” as an epithet, simple, brutal, and factual—an objective verdict. But “ugly,” as she uses it in “Ugly,” turns out to be a different kind of word: to use it to describe yourself is to evoke a whole constellation of values, many of them questionable, being brought to bear on a person whose inherent dignity resists them. It’s a word that wishes to undo itself—a word that, if we were truly to vanquish lookism, wouldn’t be needed. ♦

title: The Golden Age of the American Idiot
author: @NewYorker
content:
A new game show features celebrities competing for the title of “Nation’s Dumbest.” How did stupidity become a badge of honor?

July 23, 2026

Download a transcript.

Listen and subscribe: Apple | Spotify | Wherever You Listen

Sign up to receive our weekly cultural-recommendations newsletter.

The new game show “Nation’s Dumbest,” flips the classic “Jeopardy!” script on its head. The format: twelve famous-ish contestants are peppered with basic logic and trivia questions. The twist is that those who perform well are sent home, with the last one standing receiving the title of “Nation’s Dumbest.” On this episode of Critics at Large, Vinson Cunningham, Naomi Fry, and Alexandra Schwartz consider how the figure of the idiot has evolved over time, from Shakespearean fools—whose position of apparent ignorance allows them to speak difficult truths—to more recent “happy fools” like Austin Powers and the goofy, stunt-obsessed heroes of the “Jackass” franchise. Once a laughingstock, the idiot has reached new heights of influence in the era of A.I. summaries and the infinite scroll. Resisting stupidity can feel like an uphill battle. “Whatever it is to be smart, I’m doing this Sisyphean thing of continuing to push it up the hill, and the rock feels heavy,” Cunningham says. “The question is: is society a wind at your back, or going in the opposite direction?”
